Manufactured Intimacy.short_definition: Creating the feeling of deep closeness fast, through early confessions and painful disclosures, before the two people have any shared history to support it.
Manufactured Intimacy.core_meaning: Creating the feeling of deep closeness fast, through early confessions and painful disclosures, before the two people have any shared history to support it.
Manufactured Intimacy.expanded_definition: Manufactured intimacy is closeness produced by pace instead of time. Premature vulnerability is another name for it, used when the early disclosure is painful. Secrets, painful stories and lines like 'you get me' arrive in the first days or weeks, so the bond feels years old. Sharing pain early is not wrong, and many real bonds start that way. What stands out is closeness running well ahead of what you know, with an unspoken expectation that you will comfort, match it, or stay.
Manufactured Intimacy.plain_language_summary: Someone shares deeply and fast, often including serious pain, and you end up feeling very close to, and responsible for, a person you barely know.
Manufactured Intimacy.why_this_matters: Closeness and duty arrive before any track record can justify them. You can end up trusting at a depth your knowledge of the person cannot support, and stepping back later can feel like abandoning someone in crisis.
what_it_is: Confiding that moves faster than the relationship's age, so a two-week acquaintance carries the weight of a ten-year friendship.
Special status handed out early: you are told you are the first or only person trusted with something.
Heavy personal pain, such as trauma, loss or betrayal, shared in the first meetings, with an expectation of comfort, attention or commitment in return.
A feeling of being known that comes from the other person's stories, not from watching how they act over months.
Closeness that is hard to slow down, because slowing down feels like rejecting a gift or abandoning someone who is hurting.
what_it_sounds_like: I've never told anyone this, but I feel like I can tell you.
It's strange. I feel like I've known you my whole life.
You're the only person who has ever really listened to me.
I lost my mother last year and I just can't be alone tonight. Can you stay on the phone?
I don't know what I'd do if you pulled away too. Everyone leaves.
I'm telling you this because I know you'd never judge me. Please don't let me down.
Why would we take it slowly when this already feels so real?
I opened up to you, and you're holding back. That hurts.
what_it_is_not: Some people are simply open by temperament and tell strangers their life story without wanting anything in return.
A crisis, a shared emergency or a long night on a retreat can bring people close quickly and honestly.
Early disclosure can be someone testing whether you can be trusted with it, which is a risk they are taking rather than one they are creating.
Someone still living inside a recent loss will talk about it because it is present, not to speed anything up.
Two people who both open up at the same pace and both enjoy it are building closeness together, not having it manufactured.
Counseling, peer support and recovery groups invite fast, deep sharing in a structure with agreed limits.
this_may_be_it_when: The depth of what has been shared is far greater than the number of times you have actually met.
Confidences come with an unspoken invoice: you are expected to match them with equal depth soon.
You feel obliged to protect or stay loyal to someone before you have seen them handle any real friction.
Slowing the pace is treated as coldness, distrust or proof that you do not care.
Disclosures sharpen at the moments you seem busy, doubtful or less available.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They are fine with you sharing less than they do, and they do not keep score.
Their openness is the same with everyone in the room, not tuned to you.
When you say you would like to go slower, they say 'of course' and nothing in their warmth changes.
They asked whether you had room to listen before telling you something heavy.
The closeness has grown steadily, with behavior that matches the words.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Lonely people sometimes reach for connection quickly, and the speed comes from need rather than design.
Cultures and families differ widely on how soon personal things are talked about.
Alcohol, travel, late nights and shared adventure all make confiding feel natural for everyone involved.
Some people lack the social calibration to know how much is too much for a first meeting.
common_false_positives: Meeting someone on a long trip or at a camp, bonding deeply in a week, then staying friends afterwards.
A new friend who tells you about a divorce on the second coffee, without expecting you to do anything about it.
A newly widowed neighbor who cries when you ask how they are.
Online friendships where long, honest messages replace hours of in-person time.
discernment_questions: Could you describe how this person acts when they are tired, disappointed or told no, or only how they speak about themselves?
Does the amount of closeness match the amount of time you have really spent together?
If you said you needed things to move slower, how do you imagine they would respond?
Do you feel you owe them something because of what they told you?
Do they have other people to lean on, or are you the only one they confide in?
less_concerning_if: They share at a pace they are happy to see you match, or not match, without any change in tone.
They have friends, family or a counselor, and they ask about your life too.
You can still keep other friendships and routines without anyone minding.
more_concerning_if: Early confiding is followed by requests for money, secrecy, favors or time that you would not have agreed to a month before.
Each time you try to slow things down, a new confession or emotional crisis arrives.
You are told that you are responsible for their safety, or statements about harming themselves are used to keep you close.
pattern_over_time_signs: The same fast depth appears with each new person they meet, and earlier close friends have quietly dropped away.
Your trust keeps growing faster than your evidence, so you notice you are guessing when you would like to know.
Confessions come at predictable moments, such as right after you cancel plans or mention a doubt.
Conversations are mostly about their pain, with little room for yours, and each crisis seems bigger than the last.
Manufactured Intimacy.repair_check: Watch the speed once you have said it aloud. Someone ready to let closeness build will lean on other people too and stop asking you to match their depth. A warm apology soon followed by another round of rapid confiding leaves the pace exactly where it was.
Manufactured Intimacy.boundary_respect_check: Notice how you feel after asking for more time. If the conversation stays kind and the relationship carries on at a calmer speed, that is a good sign. If you find yourself justifying the request, or comforting them for being slowed, it has been turned into a wound.
Manufactured Intimacy.psychological_mechanism: Being handed a secret reads as a mark of status, and most of us want to answer trust with trust. Shared disclosure also produces a familiarity that normally comes from time, and a strong pull to comfort someone who is hurting. When these arrive early, the usual step of watching someone across several months can get skipped, and stepping back feels like abandoning them.
Manufactured Intimacy.possible_impact_on_receiver: Many accounts move from feeling honored, to overwhelmed, to guilty about being overwhelmed. Some gave up sleep, time and other relationships to stay reachable, then felt disoriented to find the person less known than it seemed. Others doubted their own judgment afterwards for trusting so fast, or found it hard to open up to anyone.

response_options.soft_clarification: Name the pace without blaming: 'I like talking with you, and I'm also someone who needs more time to trust. Can we go a bit slower?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Say what you cannot be: 'I can't be the only support you have. I care, and I think you deserve a counselor or friends who can give you more.'
response_options.disengagement: Let messages and meetings settle to the rate that matches how long you have actually known each other, and end calls warmly at the time you said you would.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe the first few weeks to a friend who knows you well and ask whether the speed seems as fast to them as it does in hindsight.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a colleague or client confides heavy pain, point them toward an employee assistance program, a counselor or HR, and keep your own disclosures to a level you would accept a manager reading.

Manufactured Intimacy.boundary_script: "Trusting me with this means something, and I'm sorry you went through it. I'm still getting to know you, so I'd like this to grow over time instead of all at once. That is about my pace, and it isn't a no. Who else could support you too?"
Manufactured Intimacy.safety_note: Fast closeness alone is not a danger sign. Take it more seriously when it comes with pressure to hide the relationship, to give money or housing, or when you are told you are responsible for someone's life. If someone says they may hurt themselves, do not carry that alone: contact a crisis line or emergency services for them, and tell a trusted person.
misuse_warning: Treating every quick friendship, open-hearted new partner or person sharing grief as manufactured can punish people for being warm. The label needs a mismatch between closeness and evidence, not just speed.
Using the term to avoid ever supporting someone in real crisis turns a pattern name into permission to dismiss.
Manufactured Intimacy.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Love Bombing is marked by praise, gifts and affection; this tactic can run on confiding and pain alone, with hardly a compliment. Exclusive Meaning asserts that only one person truly understands you, a line that may show up after weeks of closeness. Future Faking borrows from tomorrow with promises, while manufactured intimacy borrows from the present by speeding it up.

Silent Treatment.short_definition: Withholding all communication, warmth or answers from someone, with no stated end, until they apologize or give way to what the other person wants.
Silent Treatment.core_meaning: Withholding all communication, warmth or answers from someone, with no stated end, until they apologize or give way to what the other person wants.
Silent Treatment.expanded_definition: The silent treatment is a stretch of sustained non-response: no answers, no eye contact, messages left unread, a person in the room treated as absent. Stonewalling and withholding are other names for this one behavior, not separate tactics. It can also reach beyond talk to affection, plans, money or practical information. Everyone goes quiet sometimes. What changes the meaning is a silence with no end date, aimed at one person, that lifts only when that person apologizes or complies.
Silent Treatment.plain_language_summary: Someone stops talking to you, or takes away warmth and information, with no end in sight, until you apologize or give in. The quiet itself is the pressure.
Silent Treatment.why_this_matters: Being frozen out hurts in a way the body treats as real pain. The open-ended wait can leave you desperate to end it at any cost. Ordinary things like a reply or basic warmth turn into rewards, and the issue itself is never resolved.
what_it_is: A sustained stop to talking, replying or acknowledging someone, with no stated end.
Often shows up as ignored texts, one-word answers, leaving the room, or speaking to everyone else but you.
Can reach past talk to affection, plans, shared-account details or household information, held back until you give way.
Ends when the other person apologizes, gives in, or performs some act of making up, usually without the original issue being discussed.
Appears in couples, families, friendships and workplaces, and can last hours, days or weeks.
what_it_sounds_like: Nothing. No reply for two days after you asked a question.
I'm not talking to you until you admit what you did.
A flat 'fine' and a walk out of the room, then no words for the evening.
Don't speak to me. You know what you did.
Messages read, with no answer, while they chat happily with others.
Talking to the dog and the kids but never to you.
No reply to texts for two days after you said no to something, then a cheerful message once you changed your mind.
A partner who stops sharing the plan for the week, or the state of the shared accounts, after you disagreed.
what_it_is_not: Saying 'I'm too angry to talk about this right now. Can we pick it up after dinner?', which has a reason and a return time.
A person who goes quiet from shutting down, depression or overwhelm, and who is silent with everyone and not just you.
A break agreed on by both people during a heated argument, with a time to return.
Not sharing information because it is private, such as a friend's confidence or a medical matter that is theirs to keep.
Quiet from someone whose communication style is slow or private, and who has always been that way.
A cultural or family style of cooling off that everyone practices and that is not aimed at one person.
this_may_be_it_when: The silence starts right after you disagree or set a limit, and never has a stated end.
They speak normally to everyone else in the room.
It ends only after you apologize, bring a peace offering, or drop the issue.
You are expected to work out what you did wrong without being told.
Practical information, money or access is held back along with warmth.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They said they needed time and gave a time when they would return, and did.
The quiet is not specific to you and shows up in all their relationships.
They come back to talk the issue through, and do not require an apology first.
You feel free to approach them and they answer, even if briefly.
They are unwell, grieving or exhausted, and the quiet is clearly about that.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many people need quiet to settle down after conflict, and may not have the words yet.
Some people shut down when flooded with emotion and cannot talk, whatever their wish.
Some people were raised in homes where silence was how conflict was handled, and repeat it without noticing.
Phones die, work gets busy, and a slow reply is often just a slow reply.
common_false_positives: A partner who says 'I need an hour' and then returns to talk.
A teenager who gives short answers for a week while stressed about school, and does so with everyone.
A colleague who does not share early drafts because that is how they work with everyone.
discernment_questions: Was a reason or a return time given, or did it simply start?
Does the silence lift only when I apologize or give in?
Do they speak freely to others during the same period?
Once talk resumes, do we ever address what the silence was about?
Is practical information or money held back, or only warmth?
Do I find myself apologizing for things I do not believe I did wrong, just to end it?
less_concerning_if: The quiet is brief, announced and followed by a real conversation.
It is not aimed at you alone and does not need your apology to end.
You can still get what you need, such as money, information and a basic reply, while they cool off.
more_concerning_if: It lasts days or weeks and cuts off practical things, like telling you about money, children or housing.
They control access to money, transport, documents or your children as part of the withdrawal.
It comes with other signs of control, like checking where you are or anger when you try to reach them.
pattern_over_time_signs: You can predict that a disagreement about a certain subject will end in days of silence.
You avoid raising issues, and hold back requests and opinions, because of what will follow.
You feel a surge of relief and gratitude when they speak to you again, and you are the one who always breaks the silence first.
The stretches get longer, or happen with smaller triggers than before.
Silent Treatment.repair_check: Afterward they talk with you about the silence itself, say what they needed, and next time give a reason and a time to return. Warmth that simply resumes the moment you apologize, with the issue untouched, leaves the pattern as it was.
Silent Treatment.boundary_respect_check: Over several rounds, one question tells you more than any single reply. When you have said you will talk but do not want to be ignored for days, does the next fight end with a spoken pause and a return, or with another stretch of nothing?
Silent Treatment.psychological_mechanism: Being ignored by someone you depend on can set off a strong threat response, and the urge to end that discomfort quickly can override your own view. Without information about why or for how long, the mind may fill in the worst, and apologizing can start to feel like the only exit. Because nothing openly harmful was said, you may also doubt your own distress.
Silent Treatment.possible_impact_on_receiver: A knot in the stomach, constant phone checking, rehearsed apologies and a feeling of being invisible come up often in accounts of being frozen out. Some start to doubt whether they did something terrible, and some say they came to dread the quiet more than an open argument. Many describe walking on eggshells and agreeing to things to stop the next freeze.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the topic, not the warmth: 'You've gone quiet since Saturday. Can you tell me what's on your mind, or when you'll be ready to talk?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Separate pausing from punishing: 'I'm fine with space. I'm not fine with being ignored until I give in. Please tell me when we can talk.'
response_options.disengagement: Do not chase, plead or send a stream of messages. Keep your routines, send one calm message, and answer normally when contact resumes.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe a recent silence to a friend or counselor, including what ended it. Hearing it out loud helps check whether it lasted until you gave way.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a manager or co-worker holds back information you need to do your job, ask for it in writing and copy the request to someone senior, so a record exists.

Silent Treatment.boundary_script: "If you're upset, I'll listen and I do want to hear it. Going quiet until I give in doesn't help us fix anything, though. If you need time, tell me roughly how long, and we can pick it up then."
Silent Treatment.safety_note: Silence alone is painful pressure, not a physical threat. It matters more when you depend on the person for housing, money or care and the freeze cuts off practical information, or when it alternates with intimidation. Keep copies of your identity papers and account details somewhere private, and speak to a domestic abuse advocate or legal aid about your options.
misuse_warning: Needing space is healthy and many people go quiet from overwhelm, so labeling any pause as the silent treatment can punish someone for self-regulating, especially someone with a shutdown response.
Demanding an immediate response and then calling its absence abuse can become a form of pressure of its own.
Silent Treatment.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Emotional Blackmail spells out what you will lose if you do not comply; the silent treatment lets the quiet imply it. Hoovering is contact that returns after a break, with promises of change, while the silent treatment is contact withdrawn inside a relationship that continues. Negging keeps up contact and lowers your confidence through digs, whereas here the contact itself is the thing taken away.

The Exception Script.short_definition: Telling you that you are uniquely different from everyone around you, so that keeping that special status depends on staying close to the speaker.
The Exception Script.core_meaning: Telling you that you are uniquely different from everyone around you, so that keeping that special status depends on staying close to the speaker.
The Exception Script.expanded_definition: The exception script is flattery built on contrast: you are not like your friends, peers, family or colleagues, you are the one who truly gets it. The pedestal ploy is another label for this exact pattern. It can feel wonderful, especially if you have felt overlooked. The difficulty is a silent condition. To stay on the pedestal, you may need to keep your distance from the very people you were set apart from, and to avoid questioning the speaker.
The Exception Script.plain_language_summary: Someone praises you by putting down everyone else in your life, until being special to them starts to mean being separate from the people who know you best.
The Exception Script.why_this_matters: Being the exception means having no peers. Your worth becomes conditional on staying above the very people who might offer perspective, which can leave you with fewer places to go when something goes wrong.
what_it_is: Praise that works by comparison: you are better, deeper or more mature than the people around you.
A private status offered by someone with some influence over you, such as an older partner, a teacher, a boss, a coach or a group leader.
Often accompanied by quiet criticism of the peers you are being separated from, which makes them look like a lesser group.
A condition that is felt rather than spoken: stepping back into your group or questioning the speaker risks the special place.
Often invisible at first, since each remark alone sounds like a compliment, and particularly strong with people who feel new or misunderstood.
what_it_sounds_like: You're not like the other girls on the team. You actually take this seriously.
You're not like your friends. They could never understand you the way I do.
You're so mature for your age. The kids in your class wouldn't get you.
You're too good for that crowd. They're holding you back.
Your family doesn't appreciate you. I do.
I don't tell this to just anyone. Don't mention it to the rest of them, they'd be jealous.
Why do you waste your time on people who can't see how special you are?
Don't let them bring you down to their level.
what_it_is_not: Specific praise for something you actually did, such as 'your analysis of the data was the strongest in the group'.
A teacher or mentor who sees promise in you and also encourages you to share it and learn from peers.
Being chosen for a role on merit, which is stated openly and is the same for others in your position.
A friend who says 'you're the one I call when things get hard', a statement of closeness that leaves your other ties alone.
Two people bonding over feeling like outsiders together, without either of them asking the other to drop anyone.
A friend venting about coworkers who were truly unkind to you, without asking you to cut them off.
this_may_be_it_when: The compliment depends on others looking worse.
You are asked to keep the praise or the relationship secret from peers or family.
Warmth drops noticeably after you spend time with, or take the side of, someone in your circle.
The speaker's comments about your peers have become sharper since you got close.
You find yourself pulling away from people who used to matter to you, feeling above them.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The praise is about specific work and could be repeated in front of everyone.
They encourage you to include your peers and mention their strengths too.
You can disagree with them and still be valued.
The attention is open, such as a public award, and open to question by others.
Where they criticize someone, they give a reason and do not require you to agree.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Good teachers and coaches do notice talent and may single someone out to challenge them.
Excited early admiration often sounds comparative without being meant that way.
Someone may feel genuinely protective after hearing you were treated badly by others.
Being praised by a respected person can feel exclusive simply because they have only said it to you.
common_false_positives: A professor who says your essay stood out and suggests you apply for an honors program open to anyone.
A grandparent who calls you their favorite reader in the family and says it to each grandchild.
A new partner who admires your independence and is glad for you to keep your friends.
discernment_questions: Is the praise about what I did, or about how I compare with other people?
Am I asked to keep it quiet, or to stay away from certain people?
What happens to the warmth when I side with my peers or disagree?
Would I be comfortable with my friends or parents hearing exactly what they say about me?
Has my view of the people around me grown colder since this began?
less_concerning_if: The praise is public, specific and offered to others who earn it too.
You are encouraged to bring your peers along and keep your friendships.
You can question them without a drop in regard.
more_concerning_if: The attention comes with secrecy, private contact, gifts or a request that you not mention it to others.
The speaker has authority over you, such as a boss, teacher, coach, or an adult when you are a teenager.
Time with friends or family is met with sulking, questioning or a sudden cooling of attention.
pattern_over_time_signs: You spend less time with the group you were set apart from, and see them as lesser.
You find it harder to criticize the speaker, even privately.
Your circle shrinks until mostly people they approve of are left, and old invitations dry up.
Friends or family say they have noticed you have changed, or seem to be keeping something from them.
The Exception Script.repair_check: Look for praise that no longer needs a contrast: specific, shared with others, and given with no expectation of secrecy or distance. They also begin to welcome your peers into the picture. A bigger helping of flattery after you start pulling away is the same script with the volume up.
The Exception Script.boundary_respect_check: Try mentioning the praise to a friend, or inviting a peer along, and watch what happens. Easy acceptance suggests the attention was ordinary. Annoyance, requests for secrecy or a sudden coolness when you act like part of the group tells you something about the condition attached.
The Exception Script.psychological_mechanism: Feeling special meets a deep need to be seen, and people can become attached to a source of that feeling. If the status is framed as depending on being unlike others, a person may protect it by distancing from peers and avoiding disagreement, since both seem to threaten the special place. That can reduce the outside perspectives that would otherwise check the relationship.
The Exception Script.possible_impact_on_receiver: A warm glow, gradually mixed with worry about losing the status, is typical of what is reported, along with feeling above or apart from peers and later loneliness once friendships have drifted. Confusion and betrayal can follow on finding others were told the same thing. Some name shame at having felt superior, or at having stopped calling friends.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the specifics: 'What did I do that you liked? I'd like to hear about the work, not just how I compare with others.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline the ranking: 'I don't want to be put above the others. They're good at things too, and I'd rather not hear them criticized.'
response_options.disengagement: Step back from private, one-on-one praise and keep contact with this person to open, group or work settings.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a parent, friend or colleague you trust exactly what has been said and whether you were asked to keep it quiet. Secrecy is the part worth saying out loud.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a boss or senior colleague builds you up against your team, keep feedback in writing, share credit openly, and ask a mentor or HR how the favor will be seen if it is later withdrawn.

The Exception Script.boundary_script: "Thank you, but I don't want to be told I'm better than my friends. Tell me what you think I did well, and I'm going to keep sharing it with the people around me."
The Exception Script.safety_note: When someone with power over you, especially an adult with a young person, singles you out and asks for secrecy, gifts, private messaging or time alone, that can be a warning sign of grooming or exploitation. Watch also for anger when you see friends, or checking of your messages or money. Tell a parent, school counselor or other trusted adult, or a domestic abuse advocate, before the secret grows.
misuse_warning: Good mentors and teachers often notice and encourage special ability. Assuming that any praise for a student or employee is a script can discourage people offering honest encouragement.
Calling a partner isolating because they dislike a friend who has actually behaved badly may dismiss a reasonable concern. Look for requirements, not just comparisons.
The Exception Script.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Exclusive Meaning claims that only the speaker understands you, centered on their unique bond with you; the exception script ranks you above your peers, even with no claim about their insight. Love Bombing is a flood of attention and affection, while the exception script can be calm and quiet. Negging pulls you down with backhanded compliments; this tactic lifts you in a way that costs you your other relationships.

Dr. Jekyll/Mr. Hyde.short_definition: Showing one warm, admired face to the world and another harsh one to a particular person, which leaves nobody else seeing the treatment that person receives.
Dr. Jekyll/Mr. Hyde.core_meaning: Showing one warm, admired face to the world and another harsh one to a particular person, which leaves nobody else seeing the treatment that person receives.
Dr. Jekyll/Mr. Hyde.expanded_definition: The name comes from a well-known story about one man with two opposite selves. In everyday life it describes a split between behavior in front of others and behavior alone with one person. Performative public affection is another label for this same split. Everyone is a little different in public and private, so that alone means little. It deserves a closer look when the private side is harsh, the public side is admired, and the gap leaves the receiving person with no one who would believe them. The pattern does not show what anyone meant by it.
Dr. Jekyll/Mr. Hyde.plain_language_summary: Everyone outside the home sees a kind, attentive person. Alone with you, they are cold, controlling or cruel. Because no one else sees it, you wonder who will believe you.
Dr. Jekyll/Mr. Hyde.why_this_matters: You have no witnesses. The version other people know makes your account of the other version sound implausible, including to yourself, and anyone you might turn to has only seen the public one.
what_it_is: A sharp gap between conduct in front of others and conduct in private, aimed at one person or a small circle.
Affection or attentiveness that rises when an audience is present, and is described by others as helpful, funny, generous, reliable.
Harder to name when good phases between the harsh ones feel like proof that the harsh phases were a mistake.
Seen in couples, parents and children, bosses and employees, and religious or community leaders.
An effect created by the gap itself: the more admired the public side, the less likely the private side is to be believed.
what_it_sounds_like: A friend says, "But he's so lovely whenever I see him. Are you sure?"
In front of guests: "Isn't she wonderful? I'd be lost without her." At home, hours later, a cold silence.
"No one is going to believe you. Look how everyone sees me."
A pleasant, joking voice at the party; a flat, hostile one on the drive home.
"You've got everyone fooled into thinking I'm the bad one."
Warm texts to your family, curt and critical ones to you.
Affectionate posts and public compliments that rise on the days the private mood is worst.
what_it_is_not: A shy or tired person who is quiet at home and animated at work, with no harshness toward anyone in either place.
A professional who is polished with clients and grumpy after a long day, but who owns it and repairs it.
Someone with a hard private temper who is open about it, so others also know and can judge.
A relationship where outsiders simply have not seen ordinary arguments, which many couples keep to themselves.
A person who is guarded in public but relaxed and kind at home, which is the reverse of this split.
Someone whose public warmth is genuine and consistent with, if more understated than, their private behavior.
this_may_be_it_when: How they treat you when others are around is so different that you are unsure which one is real.
The hostile side shows up only where nobody else would see or hear it.
Friends or relatives have said they find the person lovely, and you have stopped bringing it up.
The kindness shows up after the harshness, in a way that makes you doubt your memory of it.
They have said, or you believe, that no one would take your word over theirs.
this_may_not_be_it_when: People close to you have also seen the harsh side and do not find your account surprising.
The private behavior is irritable but not cruel, and gets owned and apologized for.
The difference is one of volume or formality, such as being relaxed at home and polite at work.
A specific, understandable conflict sits behind the tension, and both of you can talk about it.
The warm public manner is also how they treat you when you are alone together.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People do act more formally in public, so a warmer social manner does not hide anything by itself.
Stress from work or health can make home the place where someone's patience runs out.
A person may hold back private arguments from friends out of embarrassment or loyalty.
Ordinary conflict is often invisible to outsiders without anyone concealing it on purpose.
common_false_positives: A teenager who is chatty with friends and withdrawn at the dinner table.
A teacher who is relaxed with students and strict in staff meetings.
Two partners with different moods after the children are asleep, both of them tired and frayed.
discernment_questions: Would people who know them be shocked, or just surprised, to hear how they speak to you in private?
Is the harshness reserved for the times when no one can hear it?
Does the warmth rise noticeably when there is an audience?
Have you stopped telling anyone because you expect not to be believed?
Do you hold dated notes, messages or recordings that show the other side, and do you feel you need them?
less_concerning_if: The difference is mostly in volume and formality, and nothing in private is hurtful.
Close friends or family have seen both sides and are not surprised by your account.
Hard moments in private are named and repaired afterward, and do not return in the same form.
more_concerning_if: You have been told directly that you would not be believed, or that you would look unstable if you spoke.
The private harshness comes with monitoring of your phone, money or movements.
They contact your friends or family to describe you as difficult before you speak to them.
pattern_over_time_signs: You decide what to share with others by how likely they are to say, "But he seems so nice."
Photos and posts show a happy home that does not match your own account of it.
Your sense of which version is real keeps flipping with the weather in the house.
You have started to keep your own record of events because nobody else holds one.
Dr. Jekyll/Mr. Hyde.repair_check: Change would look like the harsh side no longer needing a hiding place: they treat you the same when unobserved, do not object when you speak to others about what happened, and stop asking you to keep the private version private. A kinder week with the public face intact shows only a pleasant phase.
Dr. Jekyll/Mr. Hyde.boundary_respect_check: Notice whether your request is honored when nobody is watching. A boundary kept only in front of guests and dropped at home tells you what it is worth. Compare early weeks with later ones: do the private behaviors continue, even once the public manner has softened?
Dr. Jekyll/Mr. Hyde.psychological_mechanism: When most people see only the pleasant version, a person on the receiving end can start weighing their own account against everyone else's, and tends to lose. Good phases may feed hope that the harsh phases were not real, while the private ones leave no proof. Doubt about what happened, and about who would listen, can keep a person quiet.
Dr. Jekyll/Mr. Hyde.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe isolation that feels odd because they are surrounded by people who admire the other person. Some report rehearsing their account for years without telling it, and feeling an odd guilt for describing someone others like. Others say they came to dread praise of the person, and found it hardest to be congratulated for having such a partner.

response_options.soft_clarification: Say what you notice without arguing about character: 'You were gentle with my sister today, and this morning you spoke to me very differently. I'd like to understand that.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Pause the conversation when the harshness starts: 'I'm not going to continue while I'm being spoken to like this. We can try again when it is calmer.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop trying to prove the private side to people who like the public one, and keep your own dated notes where the other person cannot read them.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell one person who can listen without trying to fix or defend, such as a counselor, a domestic abuse advocate, or a friend outside the shared circle.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, write down dates, words and witnesses, and bring the record to HR or an ombuds, since a charming manner in meetings will not show up on its own.

Dr. Jekyll/Mr. Hyde.boundary_script: "I'd like us to speak to each other at home the way we do in front of other people. I'm not asking you to agree about the past, only about how we talk from here."
Dr. Jekyll/Mr. Hyde.safety_note: A split like this can sit alongside controlling behavior, threats, or physical harm that stays hidden from outsiders. Warning signs are fear of what happens after guests go home, being told you would not be believed, or having your phone, money or contacts checked. Tell a domestic abuse advocate first, and keep your records somewhere private and out of the home.
misuse_warning: Calling a person a Jekyll and Hyde because they were short with you after a hard day makes ordinary mood shifts into a case against their character. The label needs a sustained gap, not a bad evening.
Using it to tell friends that a well-liked person is secretly cruel, on the basis of your side alone, can spread a verdict that the evidence cannot yet support.
Dr. Jekyll/Mr. Hyde.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Contempt is disgust toward you and can show in public and private alike; this one depends on a gap between the two. Intimidation implies a cost for not complying and needs no split of faces. Flying Monkeys are third parties enlisted to pressure you, while here the audience usually has no idea, and is simply charmed. What is distinctive is that you have no witness who knows the private version.
